content: When the prevalence of Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis among individuals presenting with urethral discharge is approximately 60%, and molecular diagnostic assays are unavailable, treating all patients empirically for both infections would result in unnecessary treatment for 40% of cases. The Guideline Development Group has deemed this proportion acceptable, even in settings with lower prevalence rates, as treating everyone ensures that infected individuals receive appropriate therapy. This approach reduces the risk of complications and further transmission of these infections. Additionally, the group agreed that a simple syndromic treatment approach based on the presence of urethral discharge is likely to improve adherence to treatment protocols and incurs minimal additional costs compared to using history-taking and/or risk assessment with or without physical examination, while ensuring no cases are missed. Syndromic management for urethral discharge typically involves combined treatment for gonococcal and chlamydial infections, with modifications possible depending on the availability of molecular diagnostic tests. For first-line treatment of urethral discharge syndrome, the recommended therapy includes: For N. gonorrhoeae: Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly as a single dose, combined with Azithromycin 1 gram orally as a single dose. Alternatively, Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose can be used with Azithromycin 1 gram orally as a single dose. For C. trachomatis: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for seven days (if Azithromycin was not included in gonorrhea therapy), or Azithromycin 1 gram orally as a single dose. Other options include Erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for seven days or Ofloxacin 200–400 mg orally twice daily for seven days. In settings where local antimicrobial resistance data confirm susceptibility of N. gonorrhoeae to specific agents, single therapy may be considered. Options include Ceftriaxone 250 mg intramuscularly as a single dose, Cefixime 400 mg orally as a single dose, or Spectinomycin 2 grams intramuscularly as a single dose (though availability of Spectinomycin is limited). For recurrent or persistent urethral discharge, reinfection should be excluded by obtaining a thorough sexual history. If reinfection is ruled out, additional treatment for Mycoplasma genitalium and Trichomonas vaginalis may be considered. For T. vaginalis, Metronidazole 2 grams orally as a single dose or 400–500 mg twice daily for seven days is recommended. For M. genitalium, Azithromycin 500 mg orally on day 1, followed by 250 mg daily on days 2–5, is suggested. Due to increasing antimicrobial resistance to Azithromycin in N. gonorrhoeae and M. genitalium, as well as reduced susceptibility of N. gonorrhoeae to cephalosporins, the WHO is revising its treatment recommendations and dosages. Vulvovaginal symptoms, such as abnormal vaginal discharge, vulval irritation, or itching, are among the most common reasons for women to seek medical care. The three most frequent causes of vaginal discharge are bacterial vaginosis, T. vaginalis infection, and Candida albicans. In postpubertal women, N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis typically infect the endocervix rather than the vagina and may not present with vaginal discharge. If present, cervical abnormalities due to these infections may manifest as mucopurulent discharge or inflammation and friability of the cervical os. For T. vaginalis, a sexually transmitted protozoan, more than 50% of infected women experience vaginal discharge, which may be yellow and purulent. Examination findings may include vulval erythema, edema, and a frothy yellow or greenish discharge. The cervix may exhibit punctate hemorrhages, known as strawberry cervix, which is highly indicative of trichomoniasis. Molecular testing, such as nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT), is the most sensitive diagnostic method for T. vaginalis. Vaginal swabs are preferred, but endocervical samples and urine can also be used. Wet mount microscopy, while quick and inexpensive, has lower sensitivity and requires immediate examination to detect motile trichomonads. Culture methods, though more sensitive than wet mount microscopy, are less commonly used due to the availability of more advanced diagnostic techniques. For vulvovaginal candidiasis, C. albicans is responsible for approximately 90% of cases, with non-albicans species such as C. glabrata accounting for the remainder. Symptoms include vulval itching, burning, soreness, and irritation, often accompanied by a thick, curd-like white discharge. Examination findings may reveal vulval erythema, swelling, and excoriation, with adherent discharge on the vaginal walls. Diagnosis can be confirmed by Gram staining or potassium hydroxide preparation of vaginal secretions, which demonstrate gram-positive Candida species or germinated yeasts. Culture on solid media is the most sensitive diagnostic test but requires up to three days for results. Bacterial vaginosis, the most common cause of vaginal discharge in women of childbearing age, is characterized by a polymicrobial disruption of the vaginal microbiome, with reduced lactobacilli and increased anaerobic flora. Symptoms include a thin, white, homogeneous discharge and an abnormal vaginal odor. Examination findings may include discharge adherent to the vaginal walls, with a normal-appearing cervix. The whiff test, involving the addition of potassium hydroxide to vaginal fluid, may produce a characteristic fishy odor. Microscopy of a wet mount or Gram-stained smear can reveal clue cells, which are vaginal epithelial cells coated with coccobacilli and indicative of bacterial vaginosis. Cervical infections caused by N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis primarily affect the endocervix and may present as mucopurulent cervical discharge. However, these pathogens are less commonly associated with vaginal discharge. Risk factors for sexually transmitted cervical infections include younger age, multiple or new sexual partners, and a partner with an STI. At least 50% of women with gonococcal cervical infection and most with chlamydial infection are asymptomatic. Symptomatic women may report vaginal discharge, abnormal bleeding, or dysuria. Speculum examination may reveal an erythematous or eroded cervix with mucopurulent discharge. Molecular testing, particularly NAAT, is the gold standard for diagnosing N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, with self-collected vulvovaginal specimens being a reliable option.
